paragraphs: The Karamazovs’ house stood a good way from the center of town, though not quite on the outskirts. It was a pleasant old house of two stories, painted gray, with a red iron roof. Roomy and snug, it had many years of life left in it. It was full of unexpected little cupboards, closets and staircases. It also had rats, but Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t altogether mind them. “You don’t feel so lonely when you’re left by yourself in the evening,” he used to say. His habit was to send the servants off to the lodge for the night and lock himself in alone. The lodge was a big, solid building in the yard. Fyodor Pavlovitch had his cooking done there, although the house had a kitchen of its own. He couldn’t stand the smell of cooking, so winter and summer the dishes were carried across the courtyard. The house had been built for a large family, with room for five times as many people, servants included. But at the time of our story the only people living in it were Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan. The lodge held just three servants: old Grigory, his old wife Marfa, and a young man called Smerdyakov. These three deserve a few words. Of old Grigory I have already said something. He was firm and determined. Once something had convinced him, whatever the reasons (and they were often very illogical ones), that a thing was unalterably right, he went after it blindly and stubbornly. He was honest and incorruptible. His wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, had obeyed his will without question all her life. Yet after the emancipation of the serfs she had pestered him terribly. She was set on leaving Fyodor Pavlovitch and opening a little shop in Moscow with their small savings. Grigory settled the matter then, once and for all. “The woman is talking nonsense,” he said, “for every woman is dishonest.” They must not leave their old master, whatever he might be, because “that was their duty now.”
“Do you know what duty is?” he asked Marfa Ignatyevna.
“I know what the word means, Grigory Vassilyevitch. But why it’s our duty to stay here, that I’ll never understand,” Marfa answered firmly.
“Well, then, don’t understand. That’s how it’s going to be. And hold your tongue.”

And so it was. They stayed, and Fyodor Pavlovitch promised them a small wage and paid it on time. Grigory also knew that he had an undeniable hold over his master. It was true, and he was well aware of it. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a stubborn, cunning buffoon. His will was strong enough “in some of the affairs of life,” as he put it, yet in certain other emergencies he found himself, to his own surprise, extremely feeble. He knew his weaknesses and was afraid of them. In some situations a man has to keep a sharp lookout, and that’s hard without someone he can trust. Grigory was a thoroughly trustworthy man. More than once in his life Fyodor Pavlovitch had narrowly escaped a good thrashing because Grigory stepped in, and each time the old servant gave him a thorough lecture afterwards. But it wasn’t only thrashings Fyodor Pavlovitch feared. There were graver occasions, subtle and complicated ones, when a craving for someone faithful and devoted would come over him all at once, for no reason he could have explained. It was almost a sickness. In his lust he was corrupt and often cruel, like some poisonous insect. Yet when he was drunk he was sometimes overcome by a superstitious terror, a moral convulsion that almost took physical form. “My soul’s simply quaking in my throat at those times,” he used to say. In such moments he liked to feel that a strong, faithful man was close by, in the lodge if not in the room. He wanted a man who was virtuous and unlike himself, who had seen all his debauchery and knew all his secrets, and yet in his devotion was ready to overlook it all. This man was not to oppose him, and above all not to reproach him or threaten him with anything, in this world or the next. And in case of need, he was to defend him—from whom? From somebody unknown, but terrible and dangerous. What Fyodor Pavlovitch needed was to feel that there was _another_ man, an old and tried friend. In his sick moments he could call for him merely to look at his face, or perhaps to exchange a few quite irrelevant words. If the old servant wasn’t angry, Fyodor Pavlovitch felt comforted. If he was angry, he felt worse. Now and then (though very rarely) he even went to the lodge at night, woke Grigory and fetched him over for a moment. When the old man arrived, Fyodor Pavlovitch would start in on the most trivial matters, and soon send him away again, sometimes even with a joke. After Grigory had gone, Fyodor Pavlovitch would get into bed with a curse and sleep the sleep of the just. Something of the same kind had happened to him when Alyosha arrived. Alyosha “pierced his heart” by “living with him, seeing everything and blaming nothing.” More than that, Alyosha brought something his father had never known: no contempt for him at all, an unfailing kindness, and a perfectly natural, unaffected devotion to an old man who deserved it so little. All of this took the old profligate completely by surprise, since he had thrown off every family tie. It was a new and astonishing experience for a man who until then had loved nothing but “evil.” After Alyosha had left, he admitted to himself that he had learned something he hadn’t been willing to learn before.

I have already mentioned that Grigory detested Adelaïda Ivanovna, the first wife of Fyodor Pavlovitch and mother of Dmitri. Sofya Ivanovna, the poor “crazy woman,” he had protected, against his master and against anyone who happened to speak ill or lightly of her. His sympathy for the unhappy wife had become something sacred to him. Even now, twenty years later, he couldn’t stand to hear a slighting word about her from anyone, and he would stop the offender at once. Outwardly Grigory was cold, dignified and silent. He weighed his words and never spoke frivolously. At first sight you couldn’t tell whether he loved his meek, obedient wife, but he really did, and she knew it.

Marfa Ignatyevna was by no means foolish. She was probably cleverer than her husband, or at least shrewder than he in worldly matters. Even so, she had given way to him in everything, without question or complaint, from the day they married, and she respected him for his spiritual superiority. It was remarkable how little they spoke to each other in all their years together, and then only about the barest daily necessities. The grave and dignified Grigory thought over all his cares and duties alone, and Marfa Ignatyevna had long ago grown used to the fact that he didn’t need her advice. She felt that he respected her silence and took it as a sign of good sense. He had beaten her only once, and only lightly. It was in the year after Fyodor Pavlovitch’s marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna. The village girls and women, who were serfs then, had been called together in front of the house to sing and dance. They had just started “In the Green Meadows” when Marfa, a young woman at the time, skipped out and danced “the Russian Dance.” She didn’t dance it the village way. She danced it as she had learned to when she was a servant in the rich Miüsov household, in their private theater, where a dancing master from Moscow taught the actors to dance. Grigory saw how his wife was dancing. An hour later, at home in their cottage, he gave her a lesson, pulling her hair a little. And that was all: it was never repeated, and Marfa Ignatyevna gave up dancing.

God had not blessed them with children. One child was born, but it died. Grigory was fond of children and wasn’t ashamed to show it. When Adelaïda Ivanovna ran away, Grigory took the three-year-old Dmitri, combed his hair, washed him in a tub with his own hands, and looked after him for almost a year. Later he looked after Ivan and Alyosha, for which the general’s widow rewarded him with a slap in the face; but I have already told all that. The only happiness his own child ever gave him was in the waiting for its birth. When it was born, grief and horror overwhelmed him. The baby had six fingers. Grigory was so crushed that he said nothing until the day of the christening, and kept out in the garden. It was spring, and he spent three days digging the kitchen garden. The third day was the day set for the christening. By then Grigory had come to a conclusion. The clergy had gathered in the cottage and the guests had arrived, among them Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was to be godfather. Grigory walked in and suddenly announced that the baby “ought not to be christened at all.” He said it quietly and briefly, forcing the words out, with a dull, fixed stare at the priest.
“Why not?” asked the priest, good-humoredly surprised.
For some time Grigory didn’t answer. “It’s a confusion of nature,” he muttered, vaguely but firmly, plainly unwilling to say more.

They laughed and, naturally, christened the poor baby. Grigory prayed earnestly at the font, but he didn’t change his opinion of the newborn child. Still, he didn’t interfere. As long as the sickly infant lived, he hardly looked at it. In fact he tried not to notice it, and mostly stayed out of the cottage. But after a fortnight the baby died of thrush. Then he laid the child in its little coffin himself and gazed at it in deep grief. When they were filling in the shallow little grave, he fell on his knees and bowed to the ground. For years he never mentioned his child, and Marfa never spoke of the baby in front of him. Even when Grigory wasn’t there, she never spoke of it above a whisper. Marfa noticed that from the day of the burial he gave himself up to “religion.” He took to reading the _Lives of the Saints_, mostly alone and in silence, always putting on his big, round, silver-rimmed spectacles. He rarely read aloud, perhaps only in Lent. He was fond of the Book of Job. Somehow he had got hold of a copy of the sayings and sermons of “the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian,” and for years he read it doggedly. He understood very little of it, but perhaps prized and loved it all the more for that. Recently he had started listening to the teachings of the Flagellant sect that had settled in the neighborhood. They plainly shook him, but he thought it improper to go over to the new faith. His habit of theological reading gave him a look of still greater gravity.

He may have been inclined to mysticism from the start. And the birth of his deformed child and its death were followed, as though by special design, by another strange and marvelous event. As he said later, it left a “stamp” on his soul. On the very night after the burial of his child, Marfa was woken by the wail of a newborn baby. She was frightened and woke her husband. He listened, and said it sounded more like someone groaning, “it might be a woman.” He got up and dressed. It was a rather warm night in May. As he went down the steps, he heard groans clearly, coming from the garden. But the gate from the yard into the garden was locked at night, and there was no other way in, since a strong, high fence ran all the way around. Grigory went back into the house, lit a lantern and took the garden key. His wife was hysterical, still convinced she heard a child crying, and that it was her own baby crying and calling for her. He paid no attention and went into the garden in silence. There he realized at once that the groans were coming from the bath-house near the garden gate, and that they were a woman’s groans. He opened the door of the bath-house and saw a sight that turned him to stone. An idiot girl who wandered the streets, known to the whole town by the nickname Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (Stinking Lizaveta), had got into the bath-house and had just given birth. She lay dying, with the baby beside her. She said nothing, for she had never been able to speak. But her story needs a chapter to itself.
